common_name: Hardwick Hall Lily of the Valley (Yellow-Edged Variegated Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hardwick Hall is a variegated selection named for the Derbyshire estate where it was found growing in the gardens.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade. Hardwick Hall is distinguished from the plain species by broad, slightly blue-green leaves edged in a fine, irregular yellow-green margin, a more subtle and stable variegation than striped forms already common in cultivation. It carries the same intensely fragrant white bell flowers in spring and spreads by rhizome to form a dense colony, thriving in cool, moist, shaded woodland conditions. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Prolificans Double Lily of the Valley (Double-Flowered Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Prolificans is a compact, double-flowered form that produces frilly, multi-petaled bells in dense clusters rather than the single bells of the species.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade. Prolificans is a curious double-flowered sport of lily of the valley, its arching stems weighed down with unusually abundant clusters of frilly, multi-petaled white bells rather than the simple bells of the species, while retaining the same strong sweet fragrance. It grows in a smaller, more restrained clump than the species and straight majalis-type cultivars already in wide circulation, making it well suited to small woodland borders where the fuller flower display can be appreciated up close. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Giant Chinese Solomon's Seal (Arching Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; giant Chinese Solomon's seal forms rapidly expanding clumps and is one of the larger-scaled species in the genus.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade. Native to wooded slopes of southeastern China up to 6,500 feet elevation, Polygonatum cyrtonema sends up tall, gracefully arching stems hung with over a hundred pendent, tubular white flowers tipped in green, followed by clusters of black berries in fall. It expands into a substantial clump of four feet tall by three feet wide within about five years, faster and larger-scaled than many other Solomon's seal species already grown, and tolerates summer heat and humidity well. Divide congested clumps in fall every few years to control spread or increase the planting.

common_name: Gregynog Gold Ligularia (Bold-Leaf Moisture-Loving Shade Perennial)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in reliably moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from midday sun; Gregynog Gold is a robust hybrid raised at Gregynog Hall in Wales, taller and more vigorous than most Ligularia dentata cultivars.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade with shelter from midday sun and drying wind. Gregynog Gold is a vigorous hybrid bearing large, rounded, slightly wavy deep green leaves and, in mid-to-late summer, tall conical spikes of bright golden-orange daisy flowers that stand well above the foliage on stems that can reach six feet in ideal conditions. It is valued for its imposing scale in bog gardens and pondside plantings, and like other ligularias it wilts visibly during hot afternoons before recovering overnight, a sign it wants more shade or moisture rather than disease. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in full shade with consistently high humidity; Martens' spikemoss is only reliably hardy outdoors in the warmest frost-free climates and is more commonly grown as a terrarium or houseplant specimen.

directions: Plant in constantly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade, and maintain high ambient humidity of 60 percent or more since dry air quickly causes browning tips and foliage dieback. Native to Mexico and Central America, Martens' spikemoss forms a cascading mound of trailing, fern-like fronds, and the popular frosted form of this species is prized for foliage tips lightly dusted in white, giving rise to its common name. Outside its reliably hardy zones it thrives as a terrarium, vivarium, or humidity-tray houseplant, or as a groundcover for shaded, frost-free outdoor gardens, but it resents cold drafts, direct sun, and drying out between waterings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted plantlets in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Cuscutiformis is named for its thread-fine red stolons, reminiscent of the parasitic dodder vine, that carry small plantlets to root nearby.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted plantlets in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Cuscutiformis forms rosettes of rounded, deep green leaves marked with silvery veining and a maroon-red underside, and sends out fine, thread-like red stolons studded with small plantlets that root wherever they touch soil, quickly knitting together an evergreen carpet. Airy sprays of small white flowers rise above the foliage in late spring and summer. It is an excellent groundcover for shaded rock gardens, hanging baskets, and terrariums, and while somewhat less cold-hardy than the plain green species, it is otherwise easy and undemanding given consistent moisture.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Allen Bush' is a compact selection named for horticulturist Allen Bush.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled woodland light. Allen Bush is a compact, tidy selection of the native woodland groundcover green-and-gold, forming a low, dense mound of foliage smaller in scale than the species and many other named forms already in cultivation, and producing cheerful five-petaled bright yellow star-shaped flowers in an extended bloom window through spring with a second flush in the cool of fall. It spreads modestly to knit together a weed-suppressing carpet without becoming aggressive, making it a good choice for smaller woodland borders, shaded edging, or mixed groundcover plantings beneath deciduous trees and shrubs.
